metadata.title: Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls Flexibilities for Developing Human Cellular and Gene Therapy Products for a Biologics License Application: Guidance for Industry
metadata.topic: Guidance · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

candidates.statement: FDA has issued several guidances that provide CMC recommendations to sponsors developing 27 CGT products. 3 Sponsors developing CGT products should consider the CMC recommendations 28 in this guidance in addition to those guidances for industry, as applicable. This guidance 29 provides information on when CMC flexibilities may be appropriate for the development of CGT 30 products and does not comprehensively address the CMC information and data necessary to 31 support CGT product licensure under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 32 262). 33
candidates.context: This guidance describes how FDA applies flexibility to the chemistry, manufacturing, and 18 controls (CMC) requirements for human cellular and gene therapy (CGT) 1 products being 19 developed for biologics license applications (BLAs) under Title 21 of the Code of Federal 20 Regulations (CFR) Part 601 (21 CFR 601). 2 Consistent with the statutory and regulatory 21 requirements for biological products, FDA uses a flexible approach to ensuring applicable CMC 22 requirements are met for CGT products. FDA’s flexible approach serves to help expedite 23 development, review, and patient access to safe and effective CGT products to treat serious or 24 life-threatening conditions that represent significant unmet medical needs. 25 1 In this guidance, the term cellular and gene therapy (CGT) product refers collectively to cellular therapy and gene therapy products. candidates.context: This guidance applies only to CGT products regulated by the Center for Biologics Evaluation 35 and Research (CBER). This guidance does not apply to animal CGT products regulated by the 36 Center for Veterinary Medicine or to other biological products. 37 In general, FDA’s guidance documents, including this guidance, do not establish legally 42 enforceable responsibilities. Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a 43 topic and should be viewed only as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory 44 requirements are cited. The use of the word should in Agency guidances means that something 45 is suggested or recommended, but not required. 46

candidates.statement: FDA encourages sponsors of CGT products to consider the principles in this section when 75 pursuing CMC development of products for potential licensure under a BLA. To meet the 76 statutory requirement for licensure, sponsors must demonstrate that their CGT product meets the 77 applicable requirements to ensure that it is safe, pure, and potent. 10 However, FDA recognizes 78 that the unique nature of a CGT product and its development program may require a non- 79 traditional approach to satisfy these requirements. 80
candidates.context: III. FLEXIBLE APPROACHES FOR CMC DEVELOPMENT 73 FDA considers the following CMC approaches to be appropriate for sponsors to support CGT 82 product development. 11 The extent of the CMC data necessary and the suitability of a CMC 83 flexibility may vary depending on the stage of development, the manufacturing process, and the 84 product. 12 For sponsors considering pursuing a BLA, FDA may seek additional data and 85 information on a case-by-case basis to ensure that the requirements for licensure can be met. 86 Sponsors are strongly encouraged to engage with FDA early and throughout CGT product 87 development. 88

candidates.statement: Sponsors of CGT products should consider the following approaches for CGT product 92 development during clinical investigations: 93
candidates.context: A. Flexibilities During Clinical Development 90 • Implementing phase-appropriate current good manufacturing practice (CGMP). In 95 general, the production of an investigational drug 13 for use in a Phase 1 clinical trial is 96 exempt from compliance with the regulations in 21 CFR Part 211. 14 This exemption 97 generally applies to studies that are designed to establish basic safety, rather than the 98 efficacy of the drug product. 99

candidates.statement: • Developing release acceptance criteria that are consistent with the phase of the 108 investigational studies. FDA may accept relatively permissive criteria for the release of 109 early-stage investigational CGT products if such criteria do not compromise safety. 110 Sponsors should refine the product specification as additional experience is gained 111 through clinical and product characterization studies. Prior to initiating Phase 2 or 3 112 clinical investigations on the CGT product, release tests must have predefined acceptance 113 criteria. 15 , 16 FDA recommends sponsors to discuss with FDA the timeline for finalizing 114 release expectations in the investigational process, and when to establish numerical 115 release acceptance criteria in connection with clinical studies intended to provide 116 substantial evidence of effectiveness to maintain product quality and to ensure that a 117 consistently manufactured product is administered during all phases of clinical 118 investigation. 17
candidates.context: For example, FDA encourages the use of a phase-appropriate process control strategy and 101 does not expect process validation for investigational products. However, we 102 recommend that sponsors perform studies to characterize their manufacturing process 103 throughout clinical development. This approach helps sponsors gain knowledge to 104 implement an effective process control strategy, which will facilitate consistent 105 performance of the commercial manufacturing process. 106 • Using a risk-based approach to comparability studies. The manufacturing and control 121 of CGT products may present challenges due to limitations such as limited process 122 knowledge, limited product quantities, and complex manufacturing processes, which pose 123 a higher risk to product quality than conventional biological products. candidates.statement: 20 In this guidance, a specification is defined as a list of tests, references to analytical procedures, and appropriate acceptance criteria, which are numerical limits, ranges, or other criteria for the tests described. It establishes the set of criteria to which a drug substance, drug product, or materials at other stages of its manufacture should conform to be considered acceptable for its intended use. See also the guidance for industry Q6B Specifications: Test Procedures and Acceptance Criteria for Biotechnological/Biological Products (August 1999)( “Q6B Specifications Guidance” ), available at https://www.fda.gov/media/71510/download .
candidates.context: 19 See the guidance for industry Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Control Information for Human Gene Therapy Investigational New Drug Applications (January 2020), available at https://www.fda.gov/media/113760/download . 21 Assay qualification involves determining the assay’s performance characteristics (e.g., accuracy, precision, specificity, and sensitivity). Assay validation should confirm the performance characteristics of the fully-optimized assay by comparing assay performance during the validation study to appropriate pre-specified acceptance criteria for accuracy, precision, specificity, and other relevant performance characteristics. See also 21 CFR 211.165(e) and 211.194(a)(2).

PPQ is a critical step in 162 validating the performance of a commercial manufacturing process and sponsors are 163 expected to include PPQ data in their BLA submission. FDA acknowledges that 164 sponsors of CGT products may experience PPQ production limitations. FDA uses a 165 flexible, scientific, and risk-based approach to help expedite CGT product development. 166 FDA does not specify a minimum number of PPQ batches in the biologics licensing 167 requirements 24 or CGMP regulations. 25 As such, FDA recommends that sponsors justify 168 the appropriate number of PPQ batches based on context-specific factors, such as the 169 overall level of understanding of the product and process, complexity of the 170 manufacturing process, and levels of control in place. 26 Sponsors should document the 171 studies performed during the design of the manufacturing process and the control 172 strategy, and any relevant manufacturing experience from other sufficiently similar 173 products and processes, in the BLA. 174

candidates.context: C. Commercial Specification Flexibilities 185 • Developing product release strategies consistent with the nature of the product, the 190 manufacturing process, and the number of lots available at the time of BLA 191 submission. FDA recognizes that there may be situations where only a small number of 192 CGT product lots are available for analysis at the time of BLA submission, often due to 193 the inherently small patient population. In these circumstances, when appropriate and 194 while still ensuring product quality, FDA may consider flexible approaches for 195 establishing product release specifications when it is not feasible to define statistically 196

candidates.statement: • Leveraging post-approval manufacturing experience to ensure robust commercial 207 acceptance criteria. Consistent with FDA’s policies regarding change management of 208 analytical procedures, sponsors can consider discussing with FDA whether it may be 209 appropriate to commit to post-approval reevaluation of product release acceptance criteria 210 in certain circumstances (e.g., when only a small number of CGT product lots are 211 available at the time of BLA submission, and when there are data generated from 212 multiple commercial batches produced after the approval if the manufacture of the CGT 213 product demonstrates consistent product quality). 30 This approach supports the 214 development of more statistically sound acceptance criteria over time. Changes to 215 specifications after approval must be submitted in a prior approval supplement. 31
candidates.context: • Developing a scientifically supported analytical method validation strategy. For 199 validation of analytical methods used for release testing, FDA does not specify a 200 minimum number of lots to be used in the validation study. FDA may consider analytical 201 method validations using a single representative lot, when appropriate. FDA may 202 consider such a strategy if it is scientifically supported and the relevant data submitted to 203 FDA demonstrates the method to be sufficiently robust and suitable for its intended 204 use. 28 , 29 D. candidates.context: D. Additional Flexibilities 218 • Leveraging stability data to support commercial expiration dating. FDA generally 223 recommends that sponsors submit real-time stability data from three lots manufactured at 224 the commercial facility, with a minimum of six months of data. However, FDA may 225 consider an alternative number of stability lots based on a risk evaluation. In addition, 226 sponsors may use stability data from clinical lots if the lots are representative (e.g., 227 manufactured with the commercial process, using the commercial formulation, and in the 228 commercial container closure). In this case, sponsors should provide sufficient data from 229 the clinical lots to support the product’s shelf life. candidates.statement: • Seeking an exception from FDA for retaining reserve samples. Under most 238 circumstances, a manufacturer of a biologic must retain sufficient material from each lot 239 of product manufactured for six months after the expiration date. 33 However, FDA 240 recognizes that meeting this requirement may not be feasible when CGT product lots are 241 very small or manufactured for individual patients. In such circumstances, FDA may 242 consider exceptions, as appropriate and consistent with 21 CFR 600.13. 243
